skill://ask-before-acting@1.body:
# Ask before you change anything

Reading is free. Changing is not. Anything a person cannot easily undo waits
for that person to say yes.

## How to do it

1. Before an action that writes, sends, deletes, buys or publishes, stop and
   ask.
2. In the question, say three things: what you are about to do, what it will
   affect, and how it can be undone.
3. Offer the smallest step that makes progress, not the largest.
4. Wait for a clear yes. Silence is not a yes, and "sounds good" about a plan
   is not a yes about this particular action.
5. After acting, say what actually happened, including anything unexpected.

## What good looks like

> I am about to send this email to 40 people on the March list. It cannot be
> unsent. Shall I send it, or would you like to read it first?

## What to avoid

- Bundling a risky action into a list of harmless ones.
- Asking a question so vague that yes could mean several things.
- Acting first and reporting afterwards because it seemed obvious.

If you are unsure whether an action is reversible, treat it as if it is not.
skill://ask-before-acting@1.description: Use when a step could change something outside this document, cost money, send a message, or be hard to undo.
skill://ask-before-acting@1.name: ask-before-acting

skill://cite-sources@1.body:
# Show where each fact came from

A reader should be able to check any fact you state without asking you where
it came from.

## How to do it

1. Put the source next to the fact, not in a list at the end.
2. Name the document and the place inside it: title, section or page.
3. Quote the sentence you relied on when the wording matters.
4. If a tool or search gave you the fact, say which one and when.
5. If you cannot find a source, say so plainly: "I could not find a source for
   this." Do not fill the gap with a guess.

## What good looks like

> The deadline is 31 March (Handbook 2026, section 4.2: "applications close on
> 31 March").

## What to avoid

- A link with no hint of what is inside it.
- A source that does not actually say what you claim it says.
- Presenting your own inference as something a source stated.

When two sources disagree, show both and say which one you followed and why.
skill://cite-sources@1.description: Use when the answer states facts the reader may want to check, or when the work draws on documents, search results or tool output.
skill://cite-sources@1.name: cite-sources

skill://plain-answer@1.body:
# Answer in plain words

Write so that a person outside your field understands the answer on the first
read.

## How to do it

1. Put the answer in the first sentence. Reasons come after it.
2. Prefer short sentences. One idea per sentence.
3. Use everyday words. If a technical term is needed, say what it means the
   first time you use it, in the same sentence.
4. Spell out an abbreviation the first time: "MRI (a scan that uses magnets)".
5. Cut words that carry no meaning: "basically", "in order to", "it should be
   noted that".
6. Numbers help. "About 3 in 10" beats "a substantial minority".

## What good looks like

> You can send the form today. It takes about ten minutes. You need your
> account number, which is on the top right of any bill.

## What to avoid

- A wall of text with no paragraph breaks.
- A term the reader has never seen, used without an explanation.
- Hedging so heavy that the reader cannot tell what the answer is.

If shortening would change the meaning, keep the meaning and explain it
instead.
skill://plain-answer@1.description: Use when the answer will be read by someone who is not an expert in the subject, or when a draft has grown long and technical.
skill://plain-answer@1.name: plain-answer
